sectionTitle: Pressure and pressure differences in fluids (physics only)

specStatements.text: A fluid can be either a liquid or a gas.
The pressure in fluids causes a force normal (at right angles) to any surface.
The pressure at the surface of a fluid can be calculated using the equation:
pressure = (force normal to a surface)/(area of that surface)
[p = F/A]
pressure, p, in pascals, Pa
force, F, in newtons, N
area, A, in metres squared, m^2
The pressure due to a column of liquid can be calculated using the equation:
pressure = height of the column × density of the liquid × gravitational field strength
[p = h ρ g]
pressure, p, in pascals, Pa
height of the column, h, in metres, m
density, ρ, in kilograms per metre cubed, kg/m^3
gravitational field strength, g, in newtons per kilogram, N/kg (In any calculation the value of the gravitational field strength (g) will be given.)
Students should be able to explain why, in a liquid, pressure at a point increases with the height of the column of liquid above that point and with the density of the liquid.
Students should be able to calculate the differences in pressure at different depths in a liquid.
A partially (or totally) submerged object experiences a greater pressure on the bottom surface than on the top surface. This creates a resultant force upwards. This force is called the upthrust.
Students should be able to describe the factors which influence floating and sinking.
The atmosphere is a thin layer (relative to the size of the Earth) of air round the Earth. The atmosphere gets less dense with increasing altitude.

Air molecules colliding with a surface create atmospheric pressure. The number of air molecules (and so the weight of air) above a surface decreases as the height of the surface above ground level increases. So as height increases there is always less air above a surface than there is at a lower height. So atmospheric pressure decreases with an increase in height.
Students should be able to:
• describe a simple model of the Earth’s atmosphere and of atmospheric pressure
• explain why atmospheric pressure varies with height above a surface.

scopeNotes.statement: In any calculation the value of the gravitational field strength (g) will be given.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every calculation item in this topic that uses p = h ρ g states the value of g inside the question itself (g = 9.8 N/kg). No item asks a student to recall a value of g, and no item can only be answered by assuming one. Where a student substitutes g = 10 N/kg instead of the value stated, that appears as a distractor (m24) and never as the key.

concepts.definition: A fluid is a substance that can flow. A fluid can be either a liquid or a gas, so gases as well as liquids exert pressure on the surfaces they are in contact with.

The pressure in fluids causes a force normal (at right angles) to any surface. This is true whichever way the surface faces: the force on the side wall of a tank is horizontal, the force on its base is vertical, and the force on a sloping surface is at right angles to that slope.
Pressure is the force acting normal to a surface divided by the area of that surface. For a fixed force, a smaller area gives a greater pressure, and a larger area gives a smaller pressure.

concepts.term: pressure = (force normal to a surface)/(area of that surface), p = F/A
concepts.definition: The pressure at the surface of a fluid is calculated from pressure = (force normal to a surface)/(area of that surface), written p = F/A, with pressure p in pascals (Pa), force F in newtons (N) and area A in metres squared (m²). This is one of the equations you are expected to recall and apply.
The pascal is the unit of pressure. A pressure of 1 Pa is produced by a force of 1 N acting normal to an area of 1 m², so 1 Pa is 1 N/m².
F is the force acting normal to the surface, measured in newtons, N. Only the force at right angles to the surface is used; a force acting along the surface does not contribute to the pressure on it.
A is the area of the surface the force acts on, measured in metres squared, m². An area given in cm² must be converted before use: 1 m² = 10 000 cm², so divide an area in cm² by 10 000 to get m².

concepts.term: pressure = height of the column × density of the liquid × gravitational field strength, p = h ρ g
concepts.definition: The pressure due to a column of liquid is calculated from pressure = height of the column × density of the liquid × gravitational field strength, written p = h ρ g, with p in pascals (Pa), h in metres (m), ρ in kilograms per metre cubed (kg/m³) and g in newtons per kilogram (N/kg). This equation is provided in the exam, so the skill being tested is selecting it and substituting into it correctly.

h is the vertical height of the column of liquid above the point being considered, measured in metres, m. It is the depth of that point below the liquid surface. It is not the width of the container, the total volume of liquid, or the height measured up from the base.
ρ is the density of the liquid in kilograms per metre cubed, kg/m³. Densities quoted in g/cm³ must be converted before use: 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³, so water of density 1.0 g/cm³ is 1000 kg/m³.

g is the gravitational field strength in newtons per kilogram, N/kg. It is not a force, and it is not measured in newtons. In any calculation the value of g will be given in the question, so use the value stated there.

concepts.term: Why pressure increases with height of column and with density
concepts.definition: The pressure at a point in a liquid is caused by the weight of the liquid above that point. A taller column of liquid above the point means more liquid, and so a greater weight pressing down; a denser liquid has more mass in the same volume, and so also a greater weight above the point. Either change increases the pressure at that point, which is why p = h ρ g has both h and ρ as factors.

concepts.term: Difference in pressure between two depths
concepts.definition: Because p = h ρ g, the difference in pressure between two depths in the same liquid depends on the difference in the height of liquid above them: difference in pressure = difference in height × density × gravitational field strength. The answer is in pascals, Pa.

A partially (or totally) submerged object experiences a greater pressure on the bottom surface than on the top surface, because the bottom surface is deeper and so has a taller column of liquid above it. The force on the bottom surface is therefore larger than the force on the top surface, creating a resultant force upwards. This force is called the upthrust.

Whether an object floats or sinks depends on the size of the upthrust compared with the object's weight. An object floats when the upthrust is equal to its weight. An object with a density less than the density of the liquid floats, coming to rest partly submerged; an object with a density greater than the density of the liquid sinks, because even when fully submerged the upthrust is smaller than its weight. It is the comparison of the two densities that matters, not the object's size or weight on its own.

The atmosphere is a thin layer of air round the Earth — thin relative to the size of the Earth. The atmosphere gets less dense with increasing altitude, so there is no sharp upper edge; the air simply thins out.

Air molecules colliding with a surface create atmospheric pressure. Each collision gives the surface a tiny force normal to it, and the huge number of collisions every second adds up to a steady pressure on every surface exposed to the air, in every direction.

concepts.term: Why atmospheric pressure decreases with height
concepts.definition: The number of air molecules (and so the weight of air) above a surface decreases as the height of the surface above ground level increases. As height increases there is always less air above a surface than there is at a lower height, so atmospheric pressure decreases with an increase in height.

misconceptions.question: Is air a fluid?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. A fluid can be either a liquid or a gas, so air is a fluid and exerts pressure on surfaces.
misconceptions.misconception: Fluids are liquids. Gases are not fluids because you cannot pour them.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday English 'fluid' is used to mean a runny liquid, and the word appears on drink bottles and in medicine, never in connection with gases.
misconceptions.correction: In physics a fluid is anything that can flow. Gases flow, so a fluid can be either a liquid or a gas.

misconceptions.question: A tank is full of water. In which direction does the water push on the side wall of the tank?
misconceptions.correct: Horizontally, at right angles to the side wall. The pressure in fluids causes a force normal to any surface, whichever way that surface faces.
misconceptions.misconception: Fluid pressure acts downwards, because the fluid's weight pulls it down.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn that pressure at depth comes from the weight of liquid above, and weight acts downwards, so they carry that single direction over to the force on every surface.
misconceptions.correction: The weight explains how big the pressure is, not which way the force acts. At any point the pressure pushes at right angles to whatever surface is there — sideways on a wall, upwards on the underside of a submerged object.

misconceptions.question: Water flows along a pipe. Which way does the water pressure push on the pipe wall?
misconceptions.correct: At right angles to the pipe wall, outwards. Pressure causes a force normal to the surface, not a force along it.
misconceptions.misconception: The pressure pushes along the surface, in the direction the fluid is moving.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students merge the idea of pressure with the idea of flow, so the push is imagined to point wherever the fluid is going.
misconceptions.correction: Separate the two ideas. Flow is the movement of the fluid; pressure produces a force normal (at right angles) to any surface the fluid touches, whatever direction the fluid is moving.

misconceptions.question: The same force is spread over a larger area. What happens to the pressure?
misconceptions.correct: The pressure decreases, because pressure = (force normal to a surface)/(area of that surface), so a larger area on the bottom of the fraction gives a smaller pressure.
misconceptions.misconception: A larger area means a larger pressure, because the force is acting over more of the surface.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'More area' sounds like 'more of everything', and students multiply the two given numbers rather than reading the equation as a division.
misconceptions.correction: Read p = F/A as 'force shared out over the area'. Spreading the same force over more area gives each square metre less force, so the pressure falls — which is why snowshoes stop you sinking.

misconceptions.question: A force of 300 N acts normal to an area of 0.25 m². Is the answer 1200 N or 1200 Pa?
misconceptions.correct: 1200 Pa. Pressure and force are different quantities: force is measured in newtons, N, and pressure in pascals, Pa.
misconceptions.misconception: Pressure is just another word for the force pushing on something, so the answer can be given in newtons.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday speech uses 'pressure' and 'force' interchangeably ('press harder'), and both are about pushing.
misconceptions.correction: Force is the push itself, in newtons. Pressure is the force on each square metre, in pascals. A 1200 Pa answer written as 1200 N loses the mark even though the arithmetic is right.

misconceptions.question: A force of 60 N acts on an area of 20 cm². Can you write 60 ÷ 20 to get the pressure in pascals?
misconceptions.correct: No. The area must be in metres squared. 20 cm² = 20 ÷ 10 000 = 0.0020 m², so the pressure is 60 ÷ 0.0020 = 30 000 Pa.
misconceptions.misconception: You can put the area straight into p = F/A in whatever unit the question gives it in.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The equation makes no mention of units, and dividing the two numbers as printed gives a tidy-looking answer.
misconceptions.correction: For an answer in pascals, F must be in newtons and A in metres squared. Convert the area first, every time.

misconceptions.question: A block of mass 5 kg presses on a surface. Can you use 5 as the value of F in p = F/A?
misconceptions.correct: No. F must be a force in newtons. The mass in kilograms must first be turned into a weight in newtons using weight = mass × gravitational field strength.
misconceptions.misconception: The 'force' in the pressure equation is the mass of the object, because that is what is pushing down.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday use 'how heavy something is' is quoted in kilograms, so kilograms feel like the natural measure of a push.
misconceptions.correction: Check the unit of every quantity before substituting: F is in newtons, N. Kilograms measure mass, not force.

misconceptions.question: A narrow tube and a wide tank hold water to the same depth. Is the pressure at the base the same?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Pressure due to a column of liquid depends on the height of the column, the density of the liquid and the gravitational field strength — not on the width of the container or the total amount of liquid.
misconceptions.misconception: The tank has far more water in it, so the pressure at its base must be greater.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students reason from total weight rather than from weight per unit area; a bigger tank obviously contains a heavier load of water.
misconceptions.correction: The extra weight in a wide tank is spread over a proportionally wider base, so the pressure is unchanged. Only h, ρ and g appear in the equation.

misconceptions.question: Why is the pressure greater at the bottom of a deep tank of water?
misconceptions.correct: Because there is a taller column of liquid above that point, so a greater weight of water is pressing on it.
misconceptions.misconception: The water at the bottom is squashed into a smaller space, and squashed water pushes harder.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students transfer the gas model, where compressing a gas does raise its pressure, to a liquid, and picture the lower water being crushed.
misconceptions.correction: Liquids are very hard to compress, and their density is treated as constant. The pressure rises with depth because of the weight of the column above, which is exactly what p = h ρ g says.

misconceptions.question: At the same depth, is the pressure the same in water and in mercury?
misconceptions.correct: No. Pressure due to a column of liquid depends on the density of the liquid as well as the height, so the denser liquid gives the greater pressure at the same depth.
misconceptions.misconception: Only the depth matters; the liquid it is made of makes no difference.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Depth is the variable used in every classroom example, and density is an unfamiliar quantity that students do not picture as 'weight of each cubic metre'.
misconceptions.correction: Density is a factor in p = h ρ g. A denser liquid has more mass, and so more weight, in the same column, so it produces a greater pressure at the same depth.

misconceptions.question: Where does the upthrust on a submerged object come from?
misconceptions.correct: From the difference between the pressures on its surfaces: the pressure on the bottom surface is greater than on the top surface, so the upward force is larger than the downward force and there is a resultant force upwards.
misconceptions.misconception: The liquid underneath pushes the object up; there is nothing pushing down on the top of it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students notice the upward push they feel in a swimming pool and do not think about the water sitting on top of a submerged object also pushing down.
misconceptions.correction: Both surfaces are pushed. The bottom face is deeper, so the pressure and the force there are bigger. Upthrust is the difference between the two, not the bottom force alone.

misconceptions.question: A large log floats but a small nail sinks. Why?
misconceptions.correct: Because the log's density is less than the density of water and the nail's density is greater, so the log can be held up by the upthrust and the nail cannot.
misconceptions.misconception: Heavy things sink and light things float.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Most everyday floating objects a student handles are small and light, and most sinking ones are dense metals or stones, so weight and density are never separated.
misconceptions.correction: Compare densities, not weights. A steel ship weighs thousands of tonnes and floats; a steel nail weighs a few grams and sinks. What matters is the density of the object compared with the density of the liquid.

misconceptions.question: A block is floating at rest on water. How does the upthrust compare with its weight?
misconceptions.correct: They are equal. The block is at rest, so the resultant force on it is zero and the upthrust balances the weight.
misconceptions.misconception: The upthrust must be bigger than the weight, otherwise the object would not stay up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students associate 'floating' with 'winning against gravity', and a bigger upward force feels like the reason the object is not sinking.
misconceptions.correction: A bigger upthrust would accelerate the object upwards out of the water. Because a floating object stays at rest, upthrust and weight must be equal in size.

misconceptions.question: How thick is the Earth's atmosphere compared with the Earth?
misconceptions.correct: It is a thin layer relative to the size of the Earth — a thin skin of air round a very large planet.
misconceptions.misconception: The atmosphere is a huge, deep blanket, far bigger than the Earth itself.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Space feels enormously far away, and diagrams of the atmosphere are usually drawn with the layers exaggerated so that they can be labelled.
misconceptions.correction: The specification is explicit: the atmosphere is a thin layer relative to the size of the Earth. Diagrams that show it as a deep shell are not drawn to scale.

misconceptions.question: Is the air at the top of a mountain the same density as the air at sea level?
misconceptions.correct: No. The atmosphere gets less dense with increasing altitude, so mountain air is less dense than air at sea level.
misconceptions.misconception: Air is air — it has the same density everywhere in the atmosphere.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Air is invisible and feels identical from day to day, so students have no everyday evidence that it thins out with height.
misconceptions.correction: Air is squashed by the weight of the air above it, so it is most dense near the ground and becomes steadily less dense with increasing altitude.

misconceptions.question: Why is atmospheric pressure lower at the top of a mountain?
misconceptions.correct: Because there are fewer air molecules, and so less weight of air, above that surface than there is at a lower height.
misconceptions.misconception: Gravity is much weaker up a mountain, so the air presses down far less.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know gravity weakens with distance and know that astronauts float, so altitude is linked to 'less gravity' well before the numbers are considered.
misconceptions.correction: Over the height of a mountain the gravitational field strength is very nearly unchanged. What changes is the amount of air above you: as height increases there is always less air above a surface, so the pressure falls.

misconceptions.question: Air is so light. How can it press on us at all?
misconceptions.correct: Air molecules colliding with a surface create atmospheric pressure, and the column of air above any surface has a real weight — about 100 000 Pa of pressure at sea level.
misconceptions.misconception: Air weighs nothing, so atmospheric pressure must really be gravity acting directly on the surface.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A litre of air weighs almost nothing on a school balance, so students conclude air is weightless and look elsewhere for the cause of the pressure.
misconceptions.correction: Air does have mass and weight; there is simply a great deal of it above you. The pressure comes from the countless molecular collisions on the surface, and it decreases with height because less air is left above.

misconceptions.question: The density of water is 1.0 g/cm³. Can that number go straight into p = h ρ g?
misconceptions.correct: No. ρ must be in kilograms per metre cubed. 1.0 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³, and that is the value to substitute.
misconceptions.misconception: Density is density — whichever unit it is given in can be used in the equation.
misconceptions.whyItArises: g/cm³ is the unit used in density practicals, so it is the form students remember, and the equation itself does not display units.
misconceptions.correction: Convert first: multiply a density in g/cm³ by 1000 to get kg/m³. Using 1 instead of 1000 makes the answer a thousand times too small.

misconceptions.question: A diver moves from 4 m deep to 10 m deep. How much does the pressure due to the water increase?
misconceptions.correct: Use the difference in height: increase in pressure = 6 m × density × gravitational field strength.
misconceptions.misconception: You work it out from the final depth, because that is where the diver ends up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every earlier question has asked for the pressure at a depth, so students apply the same routine and substitute the one depth they can see.
misconceptions.correction: Read the question: a difference in pressure needs a difference in height. Subtract the two depths first, then multiply by ρ and g.

misconceptions.question: What is g in p = h ρ g, and what unit does it have?
misconceptions.correct: g is the gravitational field strength, in newtons per kilogram, N/kg. Its value is given in the question.
misconceptions.misconception: g is the weight of the object, measured in newtons.
misconceptions.whyItArises: g appears alongside weight in weight = mass × gravitational field strength, and both are labelled with newtons somewhere in the equation.
misconceptions.correction: Gravitational field strength is the force on each kilogram, so its unit is N/kg. It is a property of the place, not a force on an object.

misconceptions.question: Water of density 1000 kg/m³ is 12 m deep. Is the pressure 12 × 1000 = 12 000 Pa?
misconceptions.correct: No. All three factors are needed: p = h ρ g = 12 × 1000 × 9.8 = 117 600 Pa.
misconceptions.misconception: The pressure is just the height multiplied by the density; g can be dropped because it is only about gravity.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Two of the three numbers appear in the question wording as the obvious data, and g is quoted separately, so it is easily left out of the substitution.
misconceptions.correction: Write the equation out and substitute all three quantities in order. Leaving g out makes the answer about ten times too small.

misconceptions.question: A pressure of 400 Pa acts on an area of 0.20 m². How do you find the force?
misconceptions.correct: Multiply: F = p × A = 400 × 0.20 = 80 N.
misconceptions.misconception: The pressure equation is a division, so you divide the numbers whichever quantity you are asked for.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember the shape of the equation, p = F/A, rather than rearranging it, and dividing the larger number by the smaller feels safe.
misconceptions.correction: Rearrange properly. From p = F/A, F = p A and A = F/p. Only the pressure is found by dividing.

misconceptions.question: How many square metres is 20 cm²?
misconceptions.correct: 0.0020 m². There are 10 000 cm² in 1 m², so divide by 10 000.
misconceptions.misconception: 1 cm = 0.01 m, so 1 cm² = 0.01 m² and 20 cm² = 0.20 m².
misconceptions.whyItArises: The length conversion is well known and is applied once, without squaring it, because the '²' is read as part of the unit's name rather than as an instruction.
misconceptions.correction: Squaring the length conversion squares the factor too: 1 m² = 100 cm × 100 cm = 10 000 cm². Dividing by 100 instead of 10 000 makes the pressure 100 times too small.

misconceptions.question: A question states g = 9.8 N/kg. Can you use 10 N/kg instead because it is easier?
misconceptions.correct: No. In any calculation the value of the gravitational field strength will be given, and that is the value you must substitute.
misconceptions.misconception: g is always 10 N/kg — that is the number we always use.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Many early lessons round g to 10 N/kg to make the arithmetic easy, so the rounded value becomes the remembered one.
misconceptions.correction: Take g from the question every time. Using 10 instead of 9.8 shifts the answer by about 2%, which is enough to lose the accuracy mark.

misconceptions.question: Does the cold at high altitude explain the low atmospheric pressure there?
misconceptions.correct: No. Atmospheric pressure decreases with height because there are fewer air molecules, and so less weight of air, above the surface.
misconceptions.misconception: It is freezing up there, and cold air presses less hard, so the pressure is lower.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet the gas relationship between temperature and pressure and reach for it because low temperature is the most obvious feature of high altitude.
misconceptions.correction: The explanation required here is the amount of air above the surface. As height increases there is always less air above than at a lower height, so the pressure falls.

misconceptions.question: Climbers carry oxygen at high altitude. Is that because oxygen causes atmospheric pressure?
misconceptions.correct: No. All the air molecules colliding with a surface create atmospheric pressure, not the oxygen alone; the atmosphere is mostly nitrogen.
misconceptions.misconception: There is less oxygen high up, and oxygen is what makes the pressure, so the pressure is lower.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Thin air' is discussed in biology lessons and in the news in terms of oxygen for breathing, so oxygen becomes the whole story about altitude.
misconceptions.correction: Every air molecule that collides with a surface contributes to the pressure. There is less of all of it high up, because there is less air above that height.

misconceptions.question: What creates atmospheric pressure on a surface?
misconceptions.correct: Air molecules colliding with the surface create atmospheric pressure.
misconceptions.misconception: It is the wind — moving air blowing against the surface is what presses on it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The only push from air a student actually feels is the wind, and weather forecasts talk about pressure and wind in the same breath.
misconceptions.correction: Air molecules are moving in all directions all the time, and their collisions press on every surface even in still air. Wind is a separate, extra effect.

misconceptions.question: A block of wood floats on water. How much of it is below the surface?
misconceptions.correct: Part of it is below the surface. A floating object is partially submerged, and the pressure difference across its submerged surfaces provides the upthrust that balances its weight.
misconceptions.misconception: A floating object sits on top of the water with none of it below the surface.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The phrase 'floats on water' suggests resting on top, and students see the exposed part of a boat far more clearly than the hull beneath.
misconceptions.correction: The object must be partially submerged, or there would be no surfaces at different depths and so no upthrust to hold it up.

misconceptions.question: A block has a density of 700 kg/m³. Will it float?
misconceptions.correct: In water, of density 1000 kg/m³, yes — but you must compare the two densities. The same block would sink in a liquid of density 600 kg/m³.
misconceptions.misconception: You can tell whether something floats from its own density on its own.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Water is used in nearly every example, so its density becomes an invisible standard and students learn a rule of thumb such as 'floats if less than 1000'.
misconceptions.correction: Always compare the object's density with the density of the liquid it is in. Floating depends on the pair of densities, not on one number.

misconceptions.question: How do you find the difference in pressure between a depth of 0.10 m and a depth of 0.30 m?
misconceptions.correct: Use the difference in height, 0.20 m: difference in pressure = 0.20 × ρ × g.
misconceptions.misconception: You use both depths together, so you add them and use 0.40 m.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know that both numbers must be used somewhere, and adding is the operation they reach for when combining two values.
misconceptions.correction: A difference means a subtraction. Take the shallower depth away from the deeper one, then multiply by ρ and g.

misconceptions.question: Does an object weigh less when it is under water?
misconceptions.correct: No. Its weight is unchanged; the upthrust is an extra upward force, so the resultant downward force — and the reading on a spring balance — is smaller.
misconceptions.misconception: Water makes objects lighter, so the object's weight becomes smaller in the liquid.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A stone really is easier to hold under water, and the balance reading really does drop, so 'lighter' is the natural description of what is observed.
misconceptions.correction: Weight = mass × gravitational field strength, and neither changes in water. What changes is the resultant force, because the upthrust now acts upwards as well.

misconceptions.question: Sand can be poured from a bucket. Is sand a fluid?
misconceptions.correct: No. A fluid can be either a liquid or a gas. Sand is a solid, even though grains of it can be poured.
misconceptions.misconception: Anything that can be poured is a fluid.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Can flow' is the usual one-line definition of a fluid, and pouring is how students test for flowing, so powders slip into the category.
misconceptions.correction: Use the specification's definition: a fluid is a liquid or a gas. Sand is a collection of solid grains sliding over one another.

mcqs.stem: In physics, what does the word 'fluid' mean?

options.text: A fluid must be a liquid, never a gas.
options.rationale: Everyday use of 'fluid' means a runny liquid, so gases are ruled out.

options.text: A fluid is anything that can be poured.
options.rationale: Sand and sugar can be poured, so students widen 'fluid' to include powders.

options.text: A fluid must be a gas, never a liquid.
options.rationale: Students who link 'fluid' to 'completely free to move' sometimes reserve the word for gases alone.

options.text: A fluid can be either a liquid or a gas.
options.rationale: This is the definition given in the specification: both liquids and gases can flow and both exert pressure on surfaces.

mcqs.stem: A gas is sealed inside a container. In which direction does the pressure of the gas exert a force on the container walls?

options.text: Downwards on every part of the container.
options.rationale: The weight of the fluid acts downwards, so students assume every force from it does too.

options.text: Sideways along each wall surface.
options.rationale: Students who merge pressure with flow picture the push running along the surface rather than into it.

options.text: Outwards from the centre, at any angle.
options.rationale: Picturing the gas as pushing outwards from the middle gives a force meeting a flat wall at a slant, not normal to it.

options.text: At right angles to each wall surface.
options.rationale: The pressure in fluids causes a force normal (at right angles) to any surface, whichever way that surface faces.

mcqs.stem: A crate rests on the floor. It exerts a force of 300 N normal to the floor over a contact area of 0.25 m². What pressure does the crate exert on the floor?

options.text: 75 Pa
options.rationale: 300 × 0.25, from multiplying because a larger area is thought to give a larger pressure.
p = F/A = 300 ÷ 0.25 = 1200 Pa, with force in newtons and area in metres squared.
0.25 ÷ 300, from using the equation upside down.
Correct arithmetic, but labelled as a force because pressure and force are treated as the same quantity.

mcqs.stem: A pressure of 400 Pa acts normal to a surface of area 0.20 m². What is the size of the force acting normal to that surface?

options.rationale: 400 ÷ 0.20, from dividing because the pressure equation contains a division.
Rearranging p = F/A gives F = p A = 400 × 0.20 = 80 N.

options.text: 80 Pa
options.rationale: The right arithmetic with the wrong unit, from not distinguishing force from pressure.
0.20 ÷ 400, from inverting the rearrangement.

mcqs.stem: Which units must be used in p = F/A so that the pressure comes out in pascals?

options.text: F in newtons and A in centimetres squared
options.rationale: Areas are usually measured in cm² in the laboratory, so students use them unconverted.

options.text: F in kilograms and A in metres squared
options.rationale: 'How heavy' is quoted in kilograms in everyday life, so mass is offered as the force.

options.text: F in newtons and A in metres squared
options.rationale: The specification gives force, F, in newtons, N, and area, A, in metres squared, m², which together give pressure in pascals, Pa.

options.text: F in newtons and A in metres cubed
options.rationale: Confusing the unit of area with the unit of volume, which is also written with a raised index.

mcqs.stem: A drawing pin is pushed into a board. The force on its flat head and the force at its sharp point are the same size. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The pressure at the point is smaller, because the contact area is smaller.
options.rationale: Reading 'smaller area' as 'smaller everything', instead of reading p = F/A as a division.

options.text: The pressure is the same at both, because the same force acts at both ends.
options.rationale: Treating pressure as another word for force makes equal forces mean equal pressures.

options.text: The pressure at the point is greater, because the area there is smaller.
options.rationale: The same force divided by a much smaller area gives a much greater pressure, which is why the point penetrates the board.

options.text: The pressure is the same at both, because pressure depends on the material.
options.rationale: Students attribute the effect to the sharpness or hardness of the metal rather than to the area.

mcqs.stem: A force of 60 N acts normal to a surface of area 20 cm². What is the pressure on that surface?

options.text: 3 Pa
options.rationale: 60 ÷ 20, using the area in cm² without converting it to m².

options.text: 300 Pa
options.rationale: 60 ÷ 0.20, from converting with 1 cm² = 0.01 m² instead of squaring the conversion.
60 ÷ 200 000, from multiplying the area by 10 000 instead of dividing by it.

mcqs.stem: Which statement best describes the Earth's atmosphere?

options.text: A thick layer of air with the same density at all heights.
options.rationale: Air feels the same everywhere a student has been, so it is assumed to be uniform.

options.text: A thin layer of air that gets less dense with height.
options.rationale: The atmosphere is a thin layer relative to the size of the Earth, and it gets less dense with increasing altitude.

options.text: A thin layer of air that gets more dense with altitude.
options.rationale: Altitude is linked with cold, and cold air is imagined to be heavier, so the density trend is reversed.

options.text: A deep layer of air, far thicker than the Earth is wide.
options.rationale: Space feels very far away, and diagrams of the atmosphere are drawn with the layers exaggerated.

mcqs.stem: Why does atmospheric pressure decrease as the height above the ground increases?

options.text: There is less air above the surface, so less weight of air presses on it.
options.rationale: As height increases there is always less air above a surface than at a lower height, so fewer molecules and less weight of air press on it.

options.text: Gravity is much weaker high up, so the air presses on the surface less.
options.rationale: Students know gravity weakens with distance and apply that to everyday altitudes, where the change is negligible.

options.text: The air is colder high up, so its molecules press on surfaces less hard.
options.rationale: Cold is the most obvious feature of high altitude, and the gas link between temperature and pressure is borrowed.

options.text: There is less oxygen high up, and oxygen is what creates the pressure.
options.rationale: 'Thin air' is discussed in terms of oxygen for breathing, so oxygen is taken to be the whole story.

mcqs.stem: What creates atmospheric pressure on a surface?

options.text: Air molecules pushing each other sideways.
options.rationale: The molecules are pictured as pressing on one another rather than on the surface itself.

options.text: The wind blowing over the surface.
options.rationale: Wind is the only push from air a student actually feels, so it is offered as the cause.

options.text: Gravity pulling down on the surface itself.
options.rationale: Students who think air is weightless look for another cause and settle on gravity acting directly.

options.text: Air molecules colliding with the surface.
options.rationale: Air molecules colliding with a surface create atmospheric pressure, each collision giving a small force normal to the surface.

mcqs.stem: A weather balloon rises from ground level high into the atmosphere. What happens to the air outside the balloon as it rises?

options.text: The density stays the same and the atmospheric pressure falls.
options.rationale: The pressure change is accepted but the air is still imagined to be uniform all the way up.

options.text: The density falls but the atmospheric pressure stays the same.
options.rationale: The thinning of the air is known, but it is not connected to the weight of air above the surface.

options.text: The density falls and the atmospheric pressure falls as well.
options.rationale: The atmosphere gets less dense with increasing altitude, and with less air above, atmospheric pressure decreases with height.

options.text: The density rises and the atmospheric pressure rises as well.
options.rationale: Reversing both trends, from picturing the air as squashed together higher up.

mcqs.stem: A diver is 12 m below the surface of water of density 1000 kg/m³. In this question use g = 9.8 N/kg. What is the pressure due to the water at that depth?

options.rationale: 12 × 1000, with the gravitational field strength left out of the substitution.
12 × 1 × 9.8, from using the density as 1 g/cm³ rather than converting to 1000 kg/m³.
1000 × 9.8, with the height of the column left out.

mcqs.stem: Which set of units must be used in p = h ρ g to give the pressure in pascals?

options.text: h in m, ρ in g/cm³, g in N/kg
options.rationale: g/cm³ is the density unit used in practicals, so it is the one students remember.

options.text: h in m, ρ in kg/m³, g in N
options.rationale: Treating g as a force rather than as the force on each kilogram.

options.text: h in m, ρ in kg/m³, g in N/kg
options.rationale: The specification gives the height of the column in metres, the density in kilograms per metre cubed and the gravitational field strength in newtons per kilogram.

options.text: h in cm, ρ in kg/m³, g in N/kg
options.rationale: Depths are often measured in centimetres in the laboratory, so they are used unconverted.

mcqs.stem: A tank contains oil of density 900 kg/m³ to a depth of 2.5 m. In this question use g = 9.8 N/kg. What is the pressure due to the oil at the base of the tank?

options.rationale: p = h ρ g = 2.5 × 900 × 9.8 = 22 050 Pa, using the value of g given in the question.
2.5 × 900, with the gravitational field strength left out.
2.5 × 900 × 10, from using the remembered value g = 10 N/kg instead of the value stated.
900 × 9.8, with the depth of the oil left out.

mcqs.stem: Why is the pressure at a point in a liquid greater when there is a taller column of liquid above that point?

options.text: The liquid at the bottom is squashed into a smaller space.
options.rationale: The gas model is transferred to a liquid, with the lower liquid imagined as compressed.

options.text: There is a greater weight of liquid pressing down on that point.
options.rationale: A taller column contains more liquid above the point, so a greater weight acts on it and the pressure is greater.

options.text: Deeper liquid always has a greater density than shallow liquid.
options.rationale: Density and depth are run together, so the liquid is thought to change as you go down.

options.text: The liquid above has further to fall before it reaches the point.
options.rationale: Falling and impact are imported from other topics; the liquid in a tank is at rest.

mcqs.stem: A diver swims from a depth of 4.0 m to a depth of 10.0 m in water of density 1000 kg/m³. In this question use g = 9.8 N/kg. By how much does the pressure due to the water increase?

options.rationale: 1000 × 9.8 × 10.0, using the final depth alone instead of the difference in depth.
1000 × 9.8 × 4.0, using the starting depth instead of the difference.
The difference in height is 10.0 − 4.0 = 6.0 m, so the increase in pressure is 6.0 × 1000 × 9.8 = 58 800 Pa.
1000 × 9.8 × 14.0, from adding the two depths rather than subtracting them.

mcqs.stem: Why does a totally submerged object experience an upthrust?

options.text: The liquid underneath pushes up on it and nothing pushes down on it.
options.rationale: The upward push is noticed while the liquid pressing down on the top surface is forgotten.

options.text: Liquid pressure acts upwards only, so anything in a liquid is pushed up.
options.rationale: A single direction is assigned to fluid pressure, here the direction of the effect being explained.

options.text: The pressure on its bottom surface is greater than on its top surface.
options.rationale: The bottom surface is deeper, so the upward force on it exceeds the downward force on the top surface, giving a resultant force upwards called the upthrust.

options.text: The object's weight becomes smaller when it is put into the liquid.
options.rationale: A submerged object is easier to lift, so its weight is assumed to have changed.

mcqs.stem: A solid object is placed in a liquid. Under what condition does the object float?

options.text: When the object is light, whatever the liquid it is placed in.
options.rationale: Weight and density are not separated, so 'light' is taken as the test for floating.

options.text: When the upthrust on the object is greater than its weight.
options.rationale: Floating is pictured as the upward force winning, rather than as the two forces balancing.

options.text: When the object's density is less than 1000 kg/m³, always.
options.rationale: Water is used in every example, so its density becomes a fixed rule of thumb.

options.text: When the object's density is less than the liquid's density.
options.rationale: An object less dense than the liquid comes to rest partially submerged, with the upthrust equal to its weight.

mcqs.stem: The pressure due to a column of water is 4900 Pa. The water has a density of 1000 kg/m³ and g = 9.8 N/kg. What is the height of the column?

options.rationale: 4900 ÷ 1000, with the gravitational field strength left out of the rearrangement.
The right method with a place-value slip in the division.
4900 ÷ (1 × 9.8), from using the density as 1 g/cm³ instead of 1000 kg/m³.
Rearranging p = h ρ g gives h = p/(ρ g) = 4900 ÷ (1000 × 9.8) = 0.50 m.

mcqs.stem: Two open tanks are filled with water to the same depth. Tank Y is four times as wide as tank X. How does the pressure due to the water at the base of the tanks compare?

options.text: Greater in tank Y, because tank Y contains four times as much water.
options.rationale: Total weight of water is used instead of the weight of the column above each point.

options.text: Greater in tank X, because the base of tank X has a much smaller area.
options.rationale: p = F/A is applied to the whole base without noticing that the force falls with the area.

options.text: Greater in tank X, because a narrow tank squashes the water together.
options.rationale: The liquid is imagined to be compressed in a narrow container, as a gas would be.

options.text: The same in both, because the water is at the same depth in each.
options.rationale: p = h ρ g contains no term for width or volume, so equal depths of the same liquid give equal pressures.

mcqs.stem: A cube is held completely under water. Its top face is 0.10 m below the surface and its bottom face is 0.30 m below. The water has a density of 1000 kg/m³ and g = 9.8 N/kg. What is the difference in pressure between the bottom face and the top face?

options.rationale: The difference in height is 0.30 − 0.10 = 0.20 m, so the difference in pressure is 0.20 × 1000 × 9.8 = 1960 Pa. This is what produces the upthrust.
0.30 × 1000 × 9.8, using the depth of the bottom face on its own.

options.text: 980 Pa
options.rationale: 0.10 × 1000 × 9.8, using the depth of the top face on its own.
0.40 × 1000 × 9.8, from adding the two depths instead of subtracting them.

mcqs.stem: A solid block of density 700 kg/m³ is lowered into water of density 1000 kg/m³ and released. What happens to the block?

options.text: It floats with part of it below the surface of the water.
options.rationale: The block is less dense than the water, so it comes to rest partially submerged with the upthrust equal to its weight.

options.text: It floats with all of it above the surface of the water.
options.rationale: 'Floats on water' is read as resting on top, with none of the block below the surface.

options.text: It sinks, because a solid block is heavier than water.
options.rationale: Solid and heavy are equated with sinking, without comparing the two densities.

options.text: It sinks, because 700 kg/m³ is a high density for a solid.
options.rationale: The object's density is judged on its own instead of against the density of the liquid.
